analysis.one_liner: Gives workers twelve weeks of unpaid, job-protected leave for births, adoptions, and serious family illness.
analysis.headline: The bill passed the House 237-187 and the Senate by voice vote, but President George H.W. Bush vetoed it and the House fell short of the two-thirds needed to override, 232-195.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required employers with 50 or more employees to let eligible workers take up to 12 weeks of unpaid leave to have or adopt a child, care for a seriously ill child, spouse, or parent, or recover from their own serious health condition — with the right to return to their job and keep their health insurance. The leave could be unpaid, and employers could require workers to use any paid vacation or sick leave they had already earned. Both chambers passed the bill, but the President vetoed it and the House could not muster the two-thirds majority needed to make it law. (An essentially identical bill became law in 1993.)
analysis.who_benefits: Workers at employers with 50 or more employees within 75 miles who had worked at least 12 months and 1,000 hours. They would gain the right to take 12 weeks of leave for a birth, adoption, foster placement, a family member's serious illness, or their own serious health condition, and return to the same or an equivalent job, with their health insurance maintained during the leave. Federal civil service employees would get parallel rights, and the House would apply the same rules to its own employees.

how_it_helps.text: Entitles eligible employees to 12 workweeks of leave in any 12-month period for the birth or adoption of a child, to care for a child, spouse, or parent with a serious health condition, or for their own serious health condition [S6][S7].
Guarantees restoration to the same or an equivalent position with equivalent pay and benefits, and requires employers to maintain group health coverage during the leave [S6][S7].
Lets workers substitute existing paid vacation, personal, or sick leave for part of the 12 weeks, but does not require any employer to provide new paid leave [S6][S7].
Extends parallel leave rights to federal civil service employees and applies the same leave protections to employees of the House of Representatives itself [S6][S7].

analysis.who_pays: Covered employers — businesses, public agencies, and schools with 50 or more employees — bear the cost of holding jobs open, maintaining health benefits, and covering absent workers. Workers themselves bear the cost that the leave is unpaid, so many could not afford to take the full time off.

drawbacks.text: The leave is unpaid unless the worker has accrued paid leave to substitute, so a worker who needs the income may be unable to use it; the bill created a Commission on Leave to study ways of providing salary replacement [S6][S7].

Employers with fewer than 50 employees within 75 miles of a worksite are entirely excluded, leaving most small-business workers without coverage; the bill directed a commission to study the potential costs and impact on businesses employing fewer than 50 people [S6][S7].

Employers bear real compliance and coverage costs, which is the objection opponents made: they argued the mandate should be studied before taking effect, proposing in a recommittal motion a commission study and a House pilot program first; the House rejected that motion 155-264 [S7][S10][S9].

Special rules let schools require teachers to take continuous leave or transfer to an alternative position, and limit leave near the end of an academic term, and the top 10% highest-paid employees at a workplace can be denied restoration if their absence would cause substantial economic injury [S6][S7].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit — job security for new parents and seriously ill workers at a cost mostly of unpaid time and scheduling burdens for employers — is significant and the bill was written with substantial employer accommodations: no new paid leave is required, small employers are excluded, medical certification and second opinions are allowed, and spouses at the same employer share a single 12-week entitlement. The main honest criticism is that unpaid leave helps salaried and dual-income households far more than low-wage workers, who often cannot afford to take it. The bill itself acknowledged the salary-replacement problem by creating a commission to study it.

outcome.mechanism: Both chambers passed the bill, but the President vetoed it and the House override vote reached 232-195 — short of the two-thirds majority (about 290 votes) needed to enact it over his objection.

narrative.text: The House passed the bill 237-187 on May 10, 1990, after rejecting a motion to recommit that would have delayed implementation pending a study of the mandate's effects on small businesses [S11][S10][S9].
The Senate passed the bill without amendment by voice vote on June 14, 1990 [S9].
The bill was presented to the President on June 29, 1990, and vetoed the same day [S9].

On July 25, 1990, the House vote to pass the bill over the veto failed 232-195, with 194 of 256 voting House Democrats in favor but only 38 of 176 voting Republicans; a two-thirds majority was required [S12][S9].
The Labor Department, OPM, and the Justice Department had earlier provided unfavorable executive comment on the bill during committee consideration [S9].

A nearly identical Family and Medical Leave Act was enacted in 1993 after a new President took office, so the policy eventually became law two Congresses later [widely known; not in provided sources].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers covered by the mandate were better off, since the requirement never took effect, and the President's position prevailed. Workers who would have gained job-protected leave got nothing until a similar bill became law in 1993.

for.name: Rep. William (Bill) Clay
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Family and Medical Leave Act and guided it through three House committees to passage.

for.name: 151 House cosponsors
for.role: 136 of 257 House Democrats and 15 of 175 House Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, giving it broad bipartisan support from introduction.

for.name: 198 of 257 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Provided nearly all the votes for passage, 198-54, and for overriding the veto, 194-57.

for.name: Senate
for.what_they_did: Passed the bill without amendment by voice vote on June 14, 1990.

against.name: President George H.W. Bush
against.what_they_did: Vetoed the bill on June 29, 1990, after both chambers passed it.

against.name: 138 of 175 House Republicans
against.what_they_did: Voted against passage, 133-39, and voted nearly unanimously (138-38) to sustain the veto, providing the bloc that kept the override short of two-thirds.

against.name: 57 of 257 House Democrats
against.role: House Democrats who opposed the veto override
against.what_they_did: Voted against passing the bill over the President's veto.

against.name: U.S. Chamber of Commerce and business groups
against.what_they_did: Opposed the leave mandate as a burden on employers, an argument echoed in the Republican motion to recommit seeking a small-business study before implementation.

sides.party_line_note: Passage drew 198 of 257 voting Democrats but only 39 of 176 voting Republicans, and the override vote split the same way (194-57 D, 38-138 R), though 15 Republicans had cosponsored the bill and the Senate cleared it by voice vote.

industries.note: The bill would have required them to hold jobs open for 12 weeks, maintain health benefits, and cover absent workers' duties. Their cost is precisely the job security workers would gain, which is why the business lobby opposed the bill.

industries.industry: Small employers (fewer than 50 employees within 75 miles)
industries.note: They were exempted entirely, avoiding the mandate while their larger competitors bore it. Their workers, however, got no leave rights.

industries.industry: Local school districts and private schools
industries.note: Covered by the mandate but granted special rules letting them require teachers on foreseeable intermittent leave to take continuous leave or transfer to an alternative position, and to hold teachers out until the end of an academic term.

industries.industry: Health insurers and group health plans
industries.note: The bill required employers to keep workers enrolled in group health plans during leave, keeping coverage continuous and preserving the employer-based insurance system rather than creating a new public benefit.
